clue.text: Woman's tucked into ridiculously pricey dessert

indicators.note: to tuck one thing into another is to slip it inside, so one piece goes within the other
something done ridiculously is done absurdly, so the letters are thrown into a silly new order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged
a woman is referred to as her

explanation.surface: A woman indulges in an absurdly expensive pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is': the woman is tucked into the rearranged letters, after their first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Cherry pie is a baked sweet course, a classic example of an after-dinner pudding.

clue.text: Scold child with proof of age he's defaced

parts.note: ID, an identity card, is shown as proof of age

indicators.note: defaced means losing its face, the first letter

parts.note: he, with the 's read as 'is' joining it to defaced

explanation.surface: A parent tells off a youngster whose ID card has been tampered with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'he's defaced' reads as 'he is defaced': HE loses its first letter, leaving E.
explanation.definitionFit: To chide is to rebuke or reprimand, which is what scolding means.

clue.text: Allocate English vessel to take on board a Royal Marine

indicators.note: a ship taking someone on board holds them inside it, so the letters go within

parts.note: an ark is a boat, like Noah's
RM is the abbreviation for Royal Marine

explanation.surface: An English ship picks up a Royal Marine, as if assigning a passenger.
explanation.walkthrough: The marine and the 'a' go in together after the first two letters, E and A, of E+ARK.
explanation.definitionFit: To earmark funds is to set them aside or allocate them for a purpose.

clue.text: It's unknowns supporting Radiohead — splendid!

indicators.note: in a down answer, what supports sits underneath, so these letters follow the other
a head is the top or front, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the head, or first letter, of radio
taken as written
in algebra, x, y and z are the unknowns; two are used here

explanation.surface: A fan says unknown bands opening for the rock group Radiohead is a great thing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Radiohead' looks like the band but splits into Radio's head; 'It's' is IT plus 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ritzy, from the luxurious Ritz hotels, describes something showily luxurious and grand, close to splendid.

clue.text: Design for college is set in stone

parts.note: to be pro something is to be for it

indicators.note: a gem set in a ring sits within its mounting, so one piece sits within another

parts.note: jet is a black stone used in jewellery
C is the abbreviation for college

explanation.surface: A plan for a college building is carved in stone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set in stone' reads as a fixed phrase, but 'set in' places college inside the stone.
explanation.definitionFit: A project is a planned undertaking or scheme, the noun sense of design as a plan or intention.

clue.text: Iron both ways, beginning with crease and ribbon round top of vest, working well

indicators.note: read both ways means read backwards and then forwards, so the letters appear in each direction

parts.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron, here written backwards
the same symbol again, now written forwards

indicators.note: a beginning is the start, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: the first letter of the word

indicators.note: to go round something is to encircle it, so one piece wraps another

parts.note: a tie is a ribbon or cord used for binding

indicators.note: in a down answer the top is the first letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Ironing instructions: press in both directions, crease first, then tackle the ribbon round a vest, and it works.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Iron' and 'crease' sound like laundry; Fe is iron's chemical symbol, used reversed and then straight.
explanation.definitionFit: Something effective produces the intended result, so it is functioning or working well.

clue.text: Exercise with walks occasionally on top of a mountain

parts.note: PE is physical education, school exercise

indicators.note: occasionally means every so often, so only every other letter is kept

parts.note: the second and fourth letters

explanation.surface: A hiker does a workout, with the odd walk, up on a summit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On top of a mountain' looks like the setting; 'on' is only a link, and the rest is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A peak is the pointed summit of a mountain, the highest point of its outline.

clue.text: Summon soldier for parade

parts.note: to page someone is to call for them over a speaker
a soldier ant is a kind of ant

explanation.surface: An officer calls up a soldier to march on parade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soldier' wants to be a military man; crosswords often use it for an ant, from the soldier ant caste.
explanation.definitionFit: A pageant is a public procession or spectacle of costumed people, a showy display like a parade.

clue.text: Excessive pride in hideous orange car

indicators.note: something hideous is ugly and misshapen, so the letters are distorted into a new form

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A show-off drives a garish orange vehicle with far too much self-regard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hideous' seems to judge the car's paint, but it signals rearranging the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Arrogance is an overbearing sense of one's own importance, which is pride carried too far.

clue.text: Lyrics discovered in jotter Bill returned

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so the letters are read backwards
what is discovered in something was found sitting inside it, so the letters lie within the words

parts.note: the letters running across the two words

explanation.surface: Song words are found scribbled in Bill's notebook, which he got back.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'jotter Bill' from right to left and the answer appears inside it. A jotter is a small notebook.
explanation.definitionFit: A libretto is the text of an opera or musical, the words sung to the score.

clue.text: Think about body shape

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to reckon or work out
second meaning: the form of a person's physique

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like advice to consider your shape; the two phrases are separate meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb the word means to reckon or calculate; as a noun it is a person's bodily outline.

clue.text: Liberal leader's cagey about inheritance

indicators.note: a leader goes in front, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: the first letter of the word

indicators.note: to be knocked about is to be thrown around, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A party leader is evasive when asked about money left to them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like 'concerning', but it signals that the letters before it are jumbled.
explanation.definitionFit: A legacy is money or property left to someone in a will, which is what they inherit.

clue.text: Market put up inside old church

parts.note: an ex is a former thing, so ex means old

indicators.note: to be inside is to be enclosed, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: CE is the Church of England
to hang a picture is to put it up

explanation.surface: A market stall has been set up inside an old church building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old' comes first in the answer although it is not first in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: An exchange is a place where goods or shares are traded, such as a stock or corn market.

clue.text: Harpoons fish, filling ship

indicators.note: a filling sits inside a sandwich or tooth, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: SS is a steamship
the pike is a freshwater fish

explanation.surface: A whaler spears fish until they fill the ship's hold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Harpoons' looks like a plural noun but is a verb here, matching the verb form of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To spike something is to pierce it with a sharp point, exactly what a harpoon does to a fish.

clue.text: Put off by pressure working in new depots

parts.note: P is the symbol for pressure

indicators.note: to be in something is to be within it, so one piece is enclosed
something new has been remade, so these letters take a fresh order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged
a machine that is on is working

explanation.surface: Workers in the new warehouses were deterred by the stress of the job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put off' suggests discouraged, but here it means delayed, and the pressure comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: To postpone something is to delay it to a later time, the scheduling sense of the phrasal verb.

clue.text: Small women's group with case of supplies, bread and cake

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small
the Women's Institute, a British community organisation for women

indicators.note: a case is the outside shell, so only the outer letters are taken

parts.note: the first and last letters
a roll is a small loaf of bread

explanation.surface: A little women's club brings boxes of provisions, bread and cake to a bake sale.
explanation.walkthrough: The WI is famous in Britain for jam and baking, which suits the picture.
explanation.definitionFit: A Swiss roll is a thin sponge spread with jam and rolled into a cylinder, a kind of cake.

clue.text: Understand flipping idiots caught cheating

indicators.note: to catch something is to hold it, so one piece grips the other

parts.note: to twig is informal British for to understand

indicators.note: to flip something is to turn it over, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: nits are fools, British slang for idiots

explanation.surface: Someone grasps that the blasted fools were caught cheating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' reads as a mild British swear word, but it turns the fools round.
explanation.definitionFit: Twisting is informal British for swindling or defrauding someone, a twister being a crook.

clue.text: Hoping painkiller's good

parts.note: aspirin is a common painkiller
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: Someone in pain is hoping the tablet works well.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's means 'is' here, joining the painkiller to its single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Aspiring means wishing or striving to achieve something, so it shares the sense of wanting.

clue.text: List articles about Italy and Spain

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece goes round the other

parts.note: articles are items, things or objects
I is the international vehicle code for Italy
E is the international vehicle code for Spain (España)

explanation.surface: An index of newspaper pieces covering Italy and Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Articles' suggests a, an and the, but here it simply means things.
explanation.definitionFit: To itemise is to set things out one by one, which is to make a list of them.

clue.text: Suggestion Emma endlessly upset girl running around

indicators.note: around means the jumbled letters enclose the reversed piece
running suggests the letters are on the move, out of order

parts.note: the word as written

indicators.note: upset in a down clue turns the letters upside down, so they read from the bottom up
endlessly means the last letter is dropped

parts.note: the name as written

explanation.surface: Emma is upset and endlessly running around after a girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' is a reversal in this down clue, not distress, and 'running' rearranges GIRL to GLIR, which goes 'around' the reversed piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A glimmer is a faint trace or hint, as in a glimmer of hope, so a suggestion of something.

clue.text: Realise student dropped out to get less stressed

indicators.note: out signals the remaining letters are put out of order
dropped means that letter is taken out

parts.note: L is a learner, from the L-plate of a learner driver

explanation.surface: Someone realises a student has quit the course in order to relax.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dropped' removes the L ('student') from REALISE, leaving REAISE, which 'out' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: Easier here is the comparative of easy in the sense of relaxed and calm, less tense or stressed.

clue.text: Question doubtful point before getting drunk

indicators.note: before means in front of, so the first piece leads the others

parts.note: S is south, a compass point
QU is an abbreviation for question
iffy is informal for doubtful or uncertain

explanation.surface: Someone queries a dubious claim before getting tipsy.
explanation.walkthrough: The compass point goes in front of both the question and the doubtful part.
explanation.definitionFit: Squiffy is informal British slang for slightly intoxicated or tipsy after a few drinks.

clue.text: A family briefly squeeze in post-winter sports activity

indicators.note: in puts the squeeze inside the rest
briefly means cut short by the last letter

parts.note: kin are family
to press is to squeeze

explanation.surface: A family is told to fit, quickly, into an evening after a day on the slopes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'squeeze in' looks like one instruction, but 'squeeze' is the piece and 'in' places it. Après-ski is French for 'after skiing'.
explanation.definitionFit: Après-ski is the socialising and entertainment that follows a day's skiing at a resort.

clue.text: Barrels with untaxed liquor initially hidden inside cellars

indicators.note: what is hidden inside something is enclosed by it, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: vats are large barrels or tanks

indicators.note: initially means at first, so only the opening letters are taken

parts.note: the first letters of the two words

explanation.surface: Casks of smuggled spirits are stashed away in the cellars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hidden' suggests a hidden word, but here 'hidden inside' places the initial letters within the barrels.
explanation.definitionFit: Vaults are arched underground rooms used for storage, such as wine cellars beneath a building.

clue.text: Bitterness against reduced cashback

parts.note: V is short for versus, against

indicators.note: reduced means one letter is cut off the end of the money word before it is turned round

parts.note: cash is money; read back it is the word spelt backwards

explanation.surface: Resentment at a cut in a shopping refund scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cashback' hides its own reversal: MONEY read 'back', with the end 'reduced', gives ENOM after V.
explanation.definitionFit: Venom is spite or malice in speech, a bitter hostility, beyond its literal sense of a snake's poison.

clue.text: Stun with outrageous rates

indicators.note: something outrageous is wildly out of order, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Customers are left reeling by shocking prices.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outrageous' seems to judge the rates, but it signals rearranging them.
explanation.definitionFit: To taser someone is to immobilise them with an electric stun gun, so the verb means to shock senseless.

clue.text: Popular archaeological site has nothing in the shade

parts.note: what is in is fashionable, popular
a dig is an excavation site
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A crowd-pulling excavation offers no shelter from the sun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the shade' sounds like out of the sun; 'in' is only a link and the shade is a colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Indigo is a deep blue-violet colour, one of the seven colours of the rainbow, so it is a shade.

clue.text: Customs document chap provided is in French

parts.note: a chap is a man
provided that means if
est is French for is

explanation.surface: A man's paperwork at the border is in French.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is in French' looks like a description of the document, but it is the instruction to translate 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A manifest is the list of a ship's cargo or passengers presented to port officials for clearance.

clue.text: Jam's without sharpness

indicators.note: what is out has been taken away, so letters are removed

parts.note: to wedge something is to jam it in place
read as with-out: W, the abbreviation for with, is the letter taken away

explanation.surface: A preserve that lacks any tang.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' must be split into 'with' and 'out': the abbreviation for with is taken out of the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Edge means keenness or bite, as in a voice with an edge, so it names sharpness.

clue.text: Reportedly praise soldiers protecting former PM and civic dignitary

indicators.note: protecting means the praise word and the soldiers wrap around the politician, guarding her
Reportedly means the word for praise is taken as heard spoken and written another way

parts.note: to laud is to praise
OR stands for other ranks, ordinary soldiers
Theresa May was a British Prime Minister

explanation.surface: Troops guarding an ex-Prime Minister are praised, as is a city official.
explanation.walkthrough: OR, other ranks, is the usual crossword abbreviation for ordinary soldiers; Theresa May was UK Prime Minister from 2016 to 2019.
explanation.definitionFit: The ceremonial head of a city council, such as London's, is a civic dignitary.
